content: Leon Panetta tells Guardian US is risking ‘forever war’ and says Pentagon ‘turmoil’ sending message of weakness Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, Leon Panetta, the former US defense secretary, has warned, as the US president struggles to find his way out of the controversial conflict. Panetta declared in an interview that the war with Iran – launched by Trump over six months ago – risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight. title: Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns

content: Data centers are the largely unseen infrastructure behind modern life, powering everything from the apps on your phone and shows you stream to online shopping, banking and artificial intelligence . Inside these warehouse-sized facilities, thousands of servers store data, process digital requests and keep online services running around the clock. Most Americans may never see one, but they rely on them constantly, often without realizing it. "Data centers have been around for as long as technology has been around," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital. "Anytime you’re touching technology and using everything from social media to your email, all of that information, all of the data is being processed in a data center." As more of the economy moves online, data centers have become far more than a niche piece of the tech industry. They are increasingly essential infrastructure for everyday American life. The U.S. is home to roughly 4,000 operational facilities, with thousands more planned or under construction as demand for cloud computing and AI accelerates. Here are eight ways data centers quietly power the services Americans rely on every day. From Instagram and TikTok to Gmail and banking apps, data centers process and store the information behind the services people use every day. When you open an app, upload a photo, refresh your feed or send a message, your phone is connected to servers that retrieve and deliver that information in seconds. The apps may live on a screen in your hand, but much of the work happens far away inside a physical facility filled with computers running continuously. Netflix, YouTube, Spotify and other streaming platforms rely on massive computing infrastructure to deliver movies, videos and music to millions of users at once. Data centers help store enormous libraries of content and move it quickly enough to prevent the pauses and buffering that frustrate viewers. ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM Online games also rely on data centers to connect players, synchronize what is happening in a match and reduce the lag that can make a game unplayable. The more people stream, game and use data-heavy services, the more computing power those platforms need behind the scenes. Your iPhone photos, Google Drive documents and cloud backups do not just float around in cyberspace. They are stored on physical servers inside data centers, often with copies kept in multiple locations to help prevent data loss. That means a lost phone or broken laptop does not necessarily mean lost memories or work file — but it also means the cloud depends on vast amounts of real-world hardware. Search engines rely on data centers to sort through enormous amounts of information and return results in fractions of a second. Every query triggers systems that locate relevant webpages, images, maps, videos and other information before sending the results back to your device. What feels
title: 8 everyday things that would quit working without data centers
author: Fox Politics

content: Half of President Donald Trump’s MAGA base thought the Iran war was worth its economic costs in May. Now, just a little more than a third do. That precipitous, 13-point drop in just two months, according to a new POLITICO Poll , reveals how the president’s most die-hard supporters are starting to agree with the majority of Americans who have long opposed the U.S.’ involvement in the war. Additionally, 37 percent of self-identified MAGA Trump voters say the U.S. should continue its involvement only if it doesn’t increase costs, up from 29 percent who said the same in May, according to the survey, conducted by independent polling firm Public First. Nearly 1 in 5 MAGA voters believe that the U.S. should end its war in Iran, regardless of the costs. That flagging support among the president’s most loyal supporters is the clearest sign that Americans’ patience is wearing thin as the economy continues to dominate as voters’ top concern heading into a critical midterm cycle. But Trump on Monday gave little indication that he was looking for a quick end to the war. The U.S. military has pounded Iran for the last two weeks, and speaking to reporters on Tuesday the president claimed that Iranian officials “want to desperately meet” but that “until they are ready to meet in a meaningful way we have no interest in even talking.” The White House is “at a maximum level of frustration right now, and I was told by very senior people that the president is now fully aware that the only way to the victory that he wants is completely politically impossible. The American people just will not support the kind of escalation it would take at this point,” said one person close to the White House, granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. “We’ve got more dead Americans and a politically impossible situation.” This souring of the president’s base comes amid renewed hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, which have been conducting tit-for-tat strikes after the president earlier this month declared a tentative peace agreement between the two countries “over.” Two U.S. servicemembers were killed in Jordan this weekend and gas prices have climbed above $4 per gallon , underscoring the war’s impact at home. The mood among White House staff and their outside allies is grim as the president grapples with finding a path out of an unpopular and expensive war three months from a midterm election expected to turn on cost of living issues. The president was expected to spend the year on a victory tour on affordability issues, touting his popular tax cuts, Trump accounts for newborns and lower drug prices. Instead, a domestic travel schedule has been pocked by visits to Dover Air Force Base to oversee the dignified transfer of the remains of more than a dozen dead soldiers, and he has during his campaign-style rallies been forced to time and again argue to the American people that the price of war — most salient to higher prices at the pump — was worth ending Iran’s nuclear p
title: ‘A politically impossible situation’: New poll shows Trump voters losing patience with Iran war
author: Megan Messerly

content: Top military officers from a secretive command watched a speedboat cut through the waters of the Caribbean Sea, early last September. A plane above provided live video of the vessel and the 11 men on board. In the early morning hours, Adm. Frank Bradley sought the counsel of his top legal adviser , Col. Cara Hamaguchi. Then he ordered SEAL Team 6 operators to attack the packed boat. Related U.S. Military Killed Boat Strike Survivors for Not Surrendering Correctly After the vessel exploded , two helpless survivors pulled themselves onto a fragment of the overturned hull, drifting with the current for roughly 45 minutes . Bradley — then the head of the Joint Special Operations Command and now the four-star chief of Special Operations Command — again turned to Hamaguchi for guidance. Soon, a second missile screamed down, killing the survivors. Two more missiles followed in rapid succession, sinking the remnants of the boat. That strike, carried out on September 2, 2025, began a campaign of attacks that has never ceased. “It’s been a year of murders,” said a defense official who was horrified by the first strike and has remained so as the U.S. has targeted scores of so-called “drug boats” in the year since. “The Trump administration has normalized murder.” The official added: “It’s absolutely criminal.” “The Trump administration has normalized murder.”  In all, the U.S. has conducted more than 65 attacks, resulting in over 225 civilians killed in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean in the last year. The most recent strike, in the Caribbean on August 25 , killed four people. A  classified opinion  from the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel — drawn up by an interagency lawyers working group  including representatives of the CIA, State Department, White House, Department of Justice, and Defense Department — claims that narcotics on supposed drug boats are lawful military targets because they generate revenue for cartels whom the Trump administration claims are engaged in a “ non-international armed conflict ” with the United States. Attached to that secret memo is a similarly  secret list  of “designated terrorist organizations.” Related Secret Boat Strike Memo Justifies Killings By Claiming the Target Is Drugs, Not People A second government official who has reviewed the OLC opinion called it “flimsy yet expansive,” but said the Trump administration had “nonetheless managed to overstep” its bounds. The official said that despite being crafted to “excuse what is clearly murder,” the U.S. had killed people beyond those the OLC opinion claimed were legal targets. U.S. Southern Command pushed back on the allegation. “Each operation is planned and executed within the full bounds of our legal framework,” said spokesperson Steven McLoud, “ensuring that every target meets the legal criteria established by our Office of Legal Counsel.” “There is no plausible legal justification for the strik
title: The U.S. Has Killed 227 Civilians in Boat Strikes During “A Year of Murders”
author: Nick Turse

content: “We won,” ‌ President Donald Trump declared in March, less than two weeks after launching his war of choice against Iran. Claiming that nation was “very much destroyed and, even, obliterated,” Trump had already promised the conflict would bring peace to the region and, somehow, the globe. “The heavy and pinpoint bombing … will continue, uninterrupted … as long as necessary to achieve our objective of PEACE THROUGHOUT THE MIDDLE EAST AND, INDEED, THE WORLD!” Trump wrote . But more than six months and two failed ceasefires later, the floundering conflict sputters along. And you may have noticed that world peace has yet to be announced. Having again been bested in battle — the latest loss in a long-running series of meaningless victories (like over lowly Grenada), stalemates (like the forever war in Somalia ), and defeats (like conflicts in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia) — the U.S. military has slunk away from the fight in favor of an “economic D-Day” that so far seems to be little more than bluster. Trump’s other stated war aims, like Iran’s unconditional surrender and seizing its oil infrastructure, have also fallen by the wayside. In the end, the major accomplishments of Trump’s war seem to be limited to death and destruction: hundreds of U.S. casualties that the Pentagon has sought to downplay and cover-up , and thousands of Iranian deaths that the Pentagon is loath to mention or investigate , including a family of eight — five of them children, one a 20-day-old infant . But the almost 40,000 Iranians killed or wounded in the war may only scratch the surface of the true toll, as Ashley Gate writes in her latest piece for TomDispatch. The rough outlines of the ecological devastation are only just coming to light. And if history is any guide, the environmental fallout of the war may reach far into the future, affecting untold numbers of Iranians who survived the conflict and many others in generations to come. — Nick Turse, editor of TomDispatch If you haven’t yet, sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here. The Toxic Inheritance of America’s Wars Esmaeil Baqaei, the spokesperson for Iran’s Foreign Ministry, recently warned of the increasing environmental damage caused by the U.S. war, drawing attention to oil contamination in the Persian Gulf that has begun washing up on Iranian shores. “This incident is only one visible example of the extensive pollution — both overt and concealed — that has degraded the waters of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman,” he wrote on X. “Who bears responsibility for compensating these damages? Is it the nations that consume the inexpensive energy exported from our region, the shipping insurers, or the aggressors and their partners who have transformed the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman into a theater for military operations and the testing of highly destructive weaponry?” Alongside death and destruction that has killed or wounded tens of thousands of Iranians, the U.S.–Israeli war has caused massive environm
title: Ecocide in Iran
author: Ashley Gate

content: The WNBA is having a moment. Viewership is up. Attendance for this year’s WNBA All-Star Game surpassed the NBA’s All-Star Game. Games and events can be viewed in a record number of places, from broadcast to cable and streaming. And just this week, Angel Reese of the Atlanta Dream set a single-game record .  But the stories about the WNBA capturing national attention in recent weeks are about none of that. Instead, the focus has been on two retired NBA players, including Enes Kanter Freedom, who showed up courtside at an August 23 Chicago Sky–Indiana Fever game wearing a T-shirt that said “Woman: noun. adult human female.” “I don’t believe that he’s being genuine in any realm, in order to create this mass hysteria of sorts for an issue that’s actually simply a non-issue,” says Angela Perry , a WNBA content creator, tells The Intercept Briefing. “There are no trans women in the WNBA; there are none attempting to be in the WNBA.” This week on The Intercept Briefing podcast, host Jessica Washington speaks to Perry and journalist Katelyn Burns about how the premier women’s professional basketball league has found itself at the center of a right-wing manufactured panic. “The right has made such hay out of trans women in women’s sports that they need to keep inventing controversies in order to keep this issue front of mind,” says Burns who writes for the independent newsletter Burns Notice and co-hosts the Cancel Me, Daddy podcast.  “We have a midterm election coming up, and to be frank with you, the only thing that the right has done besides terrorizing immigrants is banning trans women from women’s sports. It’s at the center of almost all of their policies,” continues Burns. “They are inventing controversies about trans people in sports where there are no trans people involved.” “This is about women in general. They’re already talking about not wanting women to have the right to vote,” says Perry. “This isn’t just about sports. There’s a political party trying to scale us back to what they perceive was a time where things were better. But really, it was when women were more controlled.” “The bigger issue is that the people who think that they’re protected, it’s always going to get to the protected class eventually,” warns Perry. “Right now, the focus is trans, and people think they’re safe because ‘I’m not trans. I’m a cis woman and I’m protected.’ But it will impact you.” For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , YouTube, or wherever you listen. Jessica Washington: And I’m Jessica Washington, politics reporter at The Intercept.  AL: Jessie, in typical August fashion, it feels like things have kind of slowed down somewhat with Washington in recess amid the final
title: Right-Wing Trans Hate Comes for the WNBA
author: The Intercept Briefing

content: The George W. Bush administration and its camp followers in the media sold the Iraq War with lies and spin. Before the war, hawkish pundits such as CNN host Fareed Zakaria and New York Times columnist Thomas L. Friedman promised that it would bring reform to the Arab world. Once the war started, Fox News host Brit Hume gloated that critics got it "completely wrong," and his colleague Tony Snow declared a "relatively bloodless victory"—two statements that aged very badly as the new Iraq collapsed into decades of war, with U.S. troops in the line of fire. So it went in Iran. Pro-war journalists and TV talking heads predicted that the Iranian government would collapse at the first push. Once the war started, they ignored signs that things were not going as planned. Unlike the Iraq War, the war in Iran has not turned into a drawn-out insurgency. The U.S. did not even topple the government, instead accepting a ceasefire after four weeks. But that ceasefire did not hold. At press time, the U.S. and Iran were fighting over the Strait of Hormuz, a key chokepoint for trade that had been fully open before the war. *** Before the U.S. attacked Iran on February 28, a chorus of media personalities, including several with direct lines to President Donald Trump, argued that a war with Iran would last only a few days . Washington Post columnist Marc Thiessen predicted that the Iranian government would quickly fall because "the Iranian people are the boots on the ground." Mark Dubowitz, CEO of the neoconservative Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told The Hugh Hewitt Show that Ali Khamenei, then Iran's supreme leader, would not fight back because "that's the end of his regime." Fox News host Mark Levin claimed Iran physically couldn't fight back. Reza Pahlavi, the crown prince of Iran overthrown in the 1979 revolution, was frequently featured on Fox News as a pro-war Iranian voice. Although he had some support among Iranians, the suburban dad formerly known as prince was making wild promises he couldn't keep. In a February 12 interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel , Pahlavi urged U.S. intervention, claiming he had recruited an army of 100,000 defectors. Not a single uprising against the Iranian government happened during the war. John Podhoretz, heir to the neoconservative magazine Commentary , at least admitted that his predictions fell flat. In the first hours of the war, he wrote that the U.S. military would leave "quick work for Iranians themselves to kick the mullahs to the curb." On a Commentary podcast four months later, he said "there is no person on Earth who is going to say that America didn't lose the war." Other pundits simply refused to acknowledge when things were not going their way. Week after week, Fox News commentator Jack Keane said the war would be over in two or three more weeks. Many of these pundits' arguments were simply an appeal to shut up and trust the leader. In mid-March, retired British Army officer Richard Kemp complain
title: The Iraq War Cheerleaders Were Wrong. They're Wrong About Iran Too.
author: Matthew Petti

content: In 1989, Francis Fukuyama wrote a sweeping philosophical polemic in which he argued that liberal democratic capitalism was the only viable economic and political system. Countries would either converge on its model or drift into dysfunction. What prevented states and individuals from accepting this fate was a fear of being the Last Man, a Nietzschean term for the individual living without ideas worth dying for. A world in which liberal democracy was triumphant was, Fukuyama argued in “The End of History?,” one without the tragedy and pathos of the era of great ideologies — safe but boring.f When he expanded this essay three years later into The End of History and the Last Man , Fukuyama gave voice to a worry that this condition of placid stability may not be able to satisfy the drives of all individuals. Here he echoed G. W. F. Hegel, the philosopher from whom he took the idea of a universal history, who wrote that “within the state, heroes are no longer possible: they occur only in the absence of civilization.” In his upcoming memoir, In the Realm of the Last Man , Fukuyama makes clear that he views figures like Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump as unwilling to pay the cost of progress. They instead hearken back to a time of heroic conflict, refusing to accept the constraints of liberal democratic capitalism. Jacobin spoke to Fukuyama about his own intellectual development from a former Republican policy adviser to the Ronald Reagan administration and member of the RAND Corporation to a Democrat who now describes himself as, with some qualifications, a social democrat. In this interview, Fukuyama also discusses the transformations of the American right, what the Democratic left could learn from Trump, and from Zohran Mamdani’s successes in New York. John-Baptiste Oduor You were about sixteen in 1968 and became a conservative a few years later at Cornell. How did you think about yourself in relationship to the progressive and leftist politics of that period? Did you think you were reacting against them? Francis Fukuyama It was really my teachers at Cornell, particularly Allan Bloom — they were all students of Leo Strauss — who influenced me during that period. Strauss made a complex set of arguments, but basically he argued that the Western philosophical tradition had gotten itself into a dead end with the rise of the relativism that was the core of the teaching of people like Friedrich Nietzsche and Martin Heidegger. That was a problem because people still had moral commitments, which were necessary for society. Strauss argued that it was still possible to use human reason to come to an understanding of basic issues of good and bad that progressive thought had, in a certain way, rejected. I spent a lot of time as an undergraduate going back to Plato and Aristotle because that’s the core of the Western project to use reason to answer big questions about the nature of justice, the nature of human happiness, and so forth. That was really what I was d
title: Francis Fukuyama: The American Right Has Gone Off the Deep End
author: John-Baptiste Oduor

content: Iran threatened a “faster, heavier and more painful” response to further U.S. attacks Sunday as the six-month conflict between the two countries escalated again at sea, days after President Donald Trump dismissed the war as “ small potatoes .” Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf issued the warning after U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday, permanently disabling two and destroying another. The U.S. military said the strikes were retaliation for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps firing ballistic missiles toward a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. No American personnel were injured and the Iranian missiles did not hit the ships. Iran subsequently claimed it targeted three oil tankers and several U.S.-linked vessels in the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation. On Sunday, Tehran also claimed it struck an unmanned U.S. vessel attempting to enter the strait. U.S. Central Command denied the latter claim, calling it a “total lie.” The latest exchange marks another escalation in a conflict Trump sought to minimize just one day before the tanker strikes. “A lot of people don’t call it a war,” Trump told reporters Friday. “I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing.” Vice President JD Vance similarly said Thursday that he “ wouldn’t call it a war ,” arguing that major combat operations ended earlier this year. The conflict, which began Feb. 28 , has killed 18 U.S. service members and wounded more than 750. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has estimated the war has cost the United States at least $37.5 billion. Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter , Crash Course. Trump has also threatened renewed strikes on Iran’s nuclear infrastructure, telling reporters Friday that the U.S. could hit the underground Pickaxe Mountain site “very soon” if the administration determines Iran is conducting prohibited nuclear activity there. Meanwhile, fighting around the Strait of Hormuz is putting additional pressure on global energy supplies . Before the war, roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passed through the waterway. Iran has warned that attacks on its shipping and the continuing U.S. blockade could result in expanded strikes against American military vessels in the region. For now, neither side appears to be treating the conflict as “small potatoes.” Read more about the Iran War JD Vance denies Iran war is even a war at all Iran’s strategy to simply outlast Trump’s presidency Trump performs disappearing act to avoid Iranian threat The post Trump’s “small potatoes” Iran War keeps escalating appeared first on Salon.com .
title: Trump’s “small potatoes” Iran War keeps escalating
author: CK Smith

content: In no small part, the United States’ continued safety and stability have been made possible by two things: the peaceful transfer of power and stable military leadership. America has been respected for much of its existence as a shining light to other nations because we conduct free and fair elections and hand power from one president or one party to another with minimal drama. The U.S. has become a superpower not just because of military prowess, but because we administer that prowess with people who are sworn to protect the Constitution, not any particular political leader or party. Donald Trump threatens both our political and military stability. He continues to talk about voter fraud that never happened while promoting voter suppression in many different forms, hoping to make sure his MAGA minions stay in power after the midterm elections. He prefers not to transfer power, and will never do so willingly.  Related Abdul El-Sayed answered 9/11 question honestly. CBS attacked him As for the military, Trump has appointed a defense secretary who has indiscriminately fired qualified generals and endangered our entire military infrastructure in doing so. Trump needs to fire Pete Hegseth . Technically, Congress could impeach Hegseth (or any other Cabinet member), but don’t expect that to happen. Hell, don’t even expect Trump to fire Hegseth. Trump seldom does the right thing and won’t do it unless it is in his best interest.  Otherwise, Trump has shown no inclination to hold anyone accountable in his regime.  We see less and less of him and he makes no sense when we do. Wednesday in the Oval Office was so off-the-wall bad I thought I was watching a B-movie about a minor mobster. We are witnessing in real time an unprecedented presidential meltdown that makes the Nixon administration look like it was staffed by the founding fathers. As Trump’s cartoon reality crumbles, what is left of the press corps merely grins and asks ludicrous questions with Stepford-wife charm. Trump appeared with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and several other sycophants to proclaim that tourism is fantastic in this country and that so many people love us because we’re on top of the world. Then Trump had Duffy and various other middle-aged white men approach him, bowing and scraping, to address him like Luca Brasi addressing Don Corleone at his daughter’s wedding. Fox News host  Rachel Campos-Duffy , who is married to Sean Duffy, said on Tuesday that Trump tapped her husband to be transportation secretary “because that was all that’s left.” Apparently that’s not how Sean feels. According to him, it’s the best job in the world. Most presidents don’t care about infrastructure or transportation like Trump does, Duffy said, conveniently avoiding the fact that it was Joe Biden who pushed through a trillion-dollar infrastructure bill whose effects are visible all over the country.  Meanwhile, White House pool reporters reacted on Wednesday with nonsensic
title: It’s time for Trump to fire Pete Hegseth
author: Brian Karem

content: O ne simple rule shapes Kansas politics: Republicans win statewide. In U.S. Senate races, the GOP has prevailed without interruption for more than 90 years. But the rule has a corollary, which accounts for the occasional Democratic governor. A Republican thought to be too extreme, too ideological, or too big for their britches can be beaten by a centrist Democrat when the wind blows just right. And so, on the same August Tuesday that saw Michigan Democrats choose Abdul El-Sayed, Kansas Republicans realized their safe seat might not be so safe. Kansas Democrats had picked a man who extols moderation as a matter of faith—literally. Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of America’s largest mainline Protestant congregation, will challenge the first-term incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in November. In the handful of months since he announced his candidacy, Hamilton has defeated 10 garden-variety Democrats in the primary while setting new records for Kansas fundraising, pulling in $1 million in his first week and nearly $3.7 million in his first quarter. Political analysts continue to rate Hamilton a long shot; admittedly, they have nine decades of justification. But Marshall ticks every box that can mean trouble for otherwise-invulnerable Kansas Republicans. Full of himself even by senatorial standards (one Republican Senate colleague described him to me as a “know-it-all”), Marshall is leery of public forums where he might hear from protesters and tends to speak before thinking—a hazard of his appetite for cable-TV appearances. In nearly six years as a constituent of the senator, I have traveled from one end of Kansas to the other, and I have concluded that passionate supporters of Roger Marshall are the electoral equivalent of jackalopes: If they exist, I have never found one. Should Hamilton break the Senate’s longest GOP win streak, he would score more than an enormous off-year upset; his influence on 2028—a free-for-all to define post–Donald Trump politics—could be even larger. Because Hamilton seeks to vindicate the belief, beleaguered in today’s culture, that moderation is a good thing, not just as an electoral strategy, but as an approach to life. [ Elizabeth Bruenig: Texans will decide if Jesus was a lefty ] In Texas, James Talarico’s Christianity seems, at times, to dovetail with uncanny precision with the agenda of secular progressivism. Hamilton’s rhetoric suggests that his Democratic revival tent would be roomier, but at the same time he has so far faced relatively little pressure to translate his disposition into details. He is motivated by “compassion, a belief in safety nets for vulnerable people,” he told me, and also by “fiscal responsibility, limited government, and strong defense.” Such inoffensive straddling may be out of step with today’s politics. “People are really pissing mad, really, really pissing mad,” El-Sayed explained to Michelle Goldberg of The New York Times . A roiling left has risen to match Trump’s raging right. To w
title: What’s the Matter With Moderation?
author: David Von Drehle
